LEANDER, Texas — A 17-year-old from Leander has received a $50,000 Davidson Fellows Scholarship for developing a new way to study the growth of supermassive black holes.

Hitaishi Chillara earned the national scholarship for his project, “Connecting Supermassive Black Hole Growth to Observables: A Framework Using Cosmological Simulations and LSST Predictions.”

Chillara built a computational framework that combines several types of astronomical data to estimate the mass of supermassive black holes. His work can simplify scientists’ use of large datasets to examine the evolution of galaxies with their central black holes.

“I admire the institute’s values toward aspects of science that are often invisible at first: finding out not only what research can do, but also where its boundaries lie, so that we may ask better questions,” Chillara said. “For me, the award is an opportunity to share my habit of careful questioning, and I hope that I can inspire youth to do the same.”

Chillara attends the Texas Academy of Mathematics and Science. He has also won a silver medal in the U.S. Physics Olympiad and was selected to represent Team USA at the International Artificial Intelligence Olympiad. He plans to study astrophysics and electrical engineering.

The Davidson Institute, a Reno, Nevada-based nonprofit, awards the Davidson Fellows Scholarship to students 18 and younger whose work in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, literature or music has the potential to benefit society.

Since 2001, the program says it has awarded more than $11.4 million in scholarships to 490 students and has been recognized by U.S. News & World Report as a prestigious undergraduate scholarship program.

“The Davidson Fellows continue to demonstrate what young people can accomplish when curiosity, determination and innovation come together,” said Bob Davidson, founder of the Davidson Institute. “The 2026 Fellows have pursued challenging questions and developed meaningful work with the potential to make a lasting difference in their fields and communities.”
